15-1.title: Evaluating beyond 'looks correct'
15-1.tldr: Combine automatic metrics (exact match, F1, tests), an LLM-as-judge with a rubric for open-ended quality, and human review on a held-out set; track regressions.
points: Automatic metrics where deterministic (EM, F1, tests).
LLM-as-judge with a rubric for open-ended quality.

15-2.title: Retrieval vs generation, separately
15-2.tldr: An end-to-end score says 'wrong' but not why: if retrieval missed the doc, no generator can fix it; if the doc was retrieved, it's a generation/grounding failure.
points: A retrieval miss can't be fixed by the generator.

15-3.title: Why exact match fails
15-3.tldr: Exact match needs the output to equal the reference, so 'Paris' and 'The capital is Paris' both fail despite being correct; it's brittle to wording and format.
points: Use only on constrained answers; judge for paraphrase.

15-4.title: Recall@k
15-4.tldr: Fraction of a query's relevant documents retrieved in the top-k, averaged over queries (hit-rate when one relevant doc). A low score means retrieval is missing content.
points: Distinguishes missing content from ranking issues.

15-5.title: Precision@k
15-5.tldr: Fraction of the top-k that are relevant; trades off with recall — raising k raises recall and usually lowers precision.
points: Higher k → recall up, precision usually down.
Both can look fine while real quality is poor.

15-6.title: Why precision and recall can both look fine
15-6.tldr: Both can be low when embedding/chunking is wrong or the corpus lacks the answer — a plausible top-3 can be mostly irrelevant.
points: Corpus lacks the answer → nothing to retrieve.
Plausible output is not quality; measure it.

15-7.title: MRR
15-7.tldr: Mean of 1/rank of the first relevant result; matters when the single best hit and its position are what count.
points: MRR = mean of 1/rank of first relevant hit.
Best when one strong hit is needed (lookup/FAQ).

15-8.title: NDCG
15-8.tldr: Discounts each relevant result by log2(rank+1) and normalizes by the ideal ordering, rewarding good positions and supporting graded relevance.

15-9.title: Faithfulness vs relevance
15-9.tldr: Relevance = are the retrieved passages on-topic for the query. Faithfulness/groundedness = is the answer actually supported by the retrieved context.
points: Both are needed; they fail differently.

15-10.title: Computing faithfulness
15-10.tldr: Faithfulness = supported claims / total claims: decompose the answer into atomic claims, check each against the retrieved source (NLI or LLM judge), and average.
points: Decompose the answer into atomic claims.
Verify each against the retrieved source.

15-11.title: Measuring hallucination rate
15-11.tldr: Extract atomic claims, verify each against the retrieved context (LLM judge or NLI), and compute unsupported claims / total claims (or fraction of answers with any unsupported claim).

15-12.title: Perplexity
15-12.tldr: Perplexity = exp(-(1/N) sum log p(token_i)); lower means the text is more predictable. It compares LMs on the same text, not a task metric.
points: Lower = more predictable; compare on the same text.

15-13.title: LLM-as-judge limitations
15-13.tldr: Judges are biased (position/order, verbosity, self-preference), noisy, non-deterministic, and gameable/injectable; mitigate with position-swapping, voting, agreement reporting, and human calibration.
points: Mitigate: swap positions, vote, calibrate with humans.

15-14.title: Evaluating with no ground truth
15-14.tldr: Without gold labels: generate synthetic queries from known documents (doc = gold) for retrieval, use an LLM judge with a rubric, or pairwise/few-shot judging.
points: Synthetic queries from known docs (doc = gold).

15-15.title: Building an eval dataset
15-15.tldr: Mine real queries, then label by synthetic queries from known documents, by an LLM answering with cited chunks as gold, or by human labeling.
points: Or LLM answers with citations as gold.

15-16.title: How many eval examples
15-16.tldr: Depends on effect size and variance; ~100–200 gives a usable signal for one metric, and comparing two systems needs enough to detect the difference. Report variance/confidence, not just a mean.
points: Comparing systems needs power for the effect size.
Report confidence/variance, not a bare mean.

15-17.title: Comparing two models
15-17.tldr: Run both on the same held-out set with identical prompts/decoding, score with task metrics, and compare accuracy plus latency and cost.

15-18.title: Regression test suite
15-18.tldr: Fast deterministic unit tests on pipeline components plus a quality eval on a fixed dataset scored the same way each time; store a baseline and fail the build on a drop.
points: Quality eval on a fixed dataset.

15-19.title: Continuous production eval
15-19.tldr: Sample live traffic, score on a schedule or from feedback, and alert on quality drops — separate from error/latency monitoring; watch query drift and retrieval hit rates.
points: Sample live traffic; score on a schedule.
Alert on quality drops, not just errors.
Watch drift in queries and hit rates.

15-20.title: Detecting retrieval degradation
15-20.tldr: Monitor retrieval signals over time — zero-result rate, top-score distributions, click rate, and a periodic re-run of a frozen set — and alert on shifts, sliced per query type.
points: Periodic re-run of a frozen set.

15-21.title: High eval, users still unhappy
15-21.tldr: The eval set doesn't represent real usage: too-easy or synthetic queries, no adversarial/long-tail cases, missing slices, or a metric that rewards style over task success.
points: Eval set not representative of real usage.

15-22.title: Tying eval to business outcome
15-22.tldr: Translate quality into the business proxy it moves (task success, deflection, time-to-resolution, cost per resolution), and build a labeled bridge from the offline metric to that outcome.
points: Pick the business proxy (success, deflection, cost).
Correlate the offline metric to the proxy.
Use the offline metric as the fast proxy.

15-23.title: How do you know it's working: eval depth
15-23.tldr: 'How do you know it's working' tests evaluation depth, not confidence.

15-24.title: Building a retrieval eval set
15-24.tldr: Bootstrap with real queries from logs, then label relevance with an LLM judge, RAGAS-style (a strong model's cited chunks as gold), or synthetic queries built from known documents.
points: Label via LLM judge or a strong model's citations.
Or synthesize queries from known documents (doc = gold).

15-25.title: Testing non-deterministic agents: invariant-based assertions instead of exact outputs
15-25.tldr: Assert on structural and behavioral invariants (right tool called, correct exit path, schema valid, within budget) rather than exact output strings — those will always fail on agents.
points: Tool invariants: right tool called, call was schema-valid, no prohibited tools invoked
Termination invariants: exited within max_turns via expected path (success/escalation/budget), not exception
Schema invariants: structured output matched declared JSON schema; required fields present
Safety and cost invariants: no guardrail-blocked content executed; total tokens within budget
Jiuwen strategy: mock ModelClientABC to inject controlled responses; test each rail contract independently; use LLM-as-judge for behavioral correctness on eval set
